t: The Aerodrome card (the Aerodrome tab on the full-screen map) shows one aerodrome in detail: frequencies, tower status, runways and circuits, the ERSA FAC sheet, weather and NOTAMs.

Closest aerodrome by default. With Favour ahead on (More), aerodromes ahead of you are preferred over ones behind ("Closest ahead"). With a flight plan the card follows the plan: the next plan aerodrome once you're within 10 NM, so the inbound or overflying call is ready at the CTAF call point; from 15 NM when the active waypoint is one of that aerodrome's ERSA reporting points (e.g. ACE then YMMB), so the tower inbound call is ready; the aerodrome you just left or overflew, out to 5 NM; otherwise the closest. Pinned: tap an aerodrome on the map or in Nearby, or pick one in search. The header shows it's selected and the CTAF tile gets a CARD … ✕ badge. Back to auto (or the ✕) returns to the closest. The header says which rule applied. Heliports and hospital landing sites are hidden unless Show heliports is on. Include non-ERSA strips adds strips from other sources (tagged). The CTAF tile at the top always follows where you are, even when the card is pinned or following the plan.

Code, name, distance and an arrow pointing to it, plus the elevation. It sticks to the top while you scroll the card; once you've scrolled down it shrinks to one line. Tap the slim header to go back to the top of the card.

CTAF from ERSA. If ERSA has none: a CTAF printed on the VTC/VNC (tagged VTC or VNC), else the broadcast area frequency, else the AIP default 126.7. Towered aerodromes: ATIS, TWR, GND, DEL, APP, DEP from ERSA. Outside tower hours tower-only frequencies are struck through. Key values as chips: CTR entry altitude, circuit altitude, helicopter altitude, reporting points. Reporting points at tower aerodromes as chips with name, bearing and distance, nearest first. Tap one to go to it. ERSA local procedures: the full ERSA text (communications notes, local traffic regulations, flight procedures). With Helicopter selected in Radio calls, helicopter items are highlighted. Every value carries a source tag: green for AIP, orange for anything else. Where another source disagrees it's shown as a note, e.g. "OurAirports says …".

For a towered aerodrome that isn't in your plan or Go to and that you're not inside the zone of, the CTAF tile shows its approach unit (by sector at your altitude where ERSA lists several). An aerodrome with no approach unit in ERSA (Moorabbin) shows the tower. Once it's in your plan or Go to, or you're within 3 NM in its zone, it goes back to TWR.
With no aerodrome within 10 NM, the CTAF tile shows the broadcast area frequency (e.g. Abrolhos 127.1) or the area frequency at your altitude. The card still shows the closest aerodrome.

Where ERSA's procedure text ties a tower frequency to a side, it is labelled with that side and the ERSA text is quoted under it. At Moorabbin, 118.1 is East ("DEP to the E call 118.1", "ARR from E must call 118.1") and 123.0 is West ("DEP to the W call 123.0", "report at CARR on 123.0 … western circuit"). Which side: your bearing from the field. Over the field: the side of your next plan waypoint; else the side you arrived from (kept 3 minutes); else your track after take-off; else "see ATIS". Reporting-point rules win: "When RWY 17 or 35 in use, ARR VFR ACFT from the S should track via and report at CARR on 123.0" applies when you're heading for CARR, within 3 NM of it, or south of the field. So Carrum gives TWR W 123.0 · via CARR (RWY 17/35). Pick another runway in Radio calls and it goes back to the side rule. Departing: the side of the first plan point after the aerodrome. ERSA's COMM line and the VTC only list "TWR 118.1 / 123.0". The East/West labels come from ERSA's procedure text. The ATIS has the final word.

Read from ERSA's TWR HR notes, in local time with daylight saving by state. Unknown hours: the tower is assumed active. Outside tower hours the card switches to CTAF calls. Where ERSA says plainly "Outside TWR HR airspace becomes Class G" (Moorabbin, Bankstown, Archerfield, Parafield, Jandakot, Camden and others) the zone is shown as class G. Avalon's zone is also dropped after hours, leaving the DAH's class E steps above 700 ft AGL. Reversions with conditions (Albury, Gold Coast, Tamworth and others) stay as published. You can force Tower or CTAF in Radio calls. Public holidays and NOTAM changes to tower hours aren't known to the app. Confirm on the ATIS.

Diagram: runways to scale with their designators. You're an arrow, or on the edge with your distance when further out, so you can see which side you're joining from. It follows the map's track-up or north-up setting. List: designator, length, surface and right-hand circuits, e.g. "17L/35R 1,341 m sealed 35R RH". Tap an RH tag for ERSA's conditions. Other circuits are left-hand unless ERSA says otherwise. Right-hand circuits from ERSA, including "all circuits to the WEST" notes (Lilydale: RWY 18 right, 36 left by day; the reverse at night). Source: DAH runway thresholds for certified aerodromes; others drawn from ERSA's bearing and length (or the designator), dashed and labelled "schematic".

Under the name, ERSA FAC YMMB · 7 pages opens that aerodrome's ERSA pages in the app, scrolled to its entry. Zoom doubles the width; Open PDF hands it to the phone's own viewer. It's from the same ERSA cycle as the frequencies. Each sheet is stored when first opened, and those for your plan and Go to aerodromes are fetched in the background with signal so they open offline. Aerodromes without an ERSA entry have no button.

From the NAIPS briefing you load (tick weather in the NAIPS area briefing). It ages with the briefing: check the time on each report. ATIS first: from the briefing (runway, wind, cloud, QNH, operational information; changed fields highlighted; an old ATIS flagged), or ATIS heard hhmmZ when you captured it with Listen to ATIS (see ATIS capture). Area QNH for the area. METAR decoded: wind, QNH, temperature and dew point, density altitude at the aerodrome, and the crosswind and headwind for each runway (magnetic wind, best runway first). TAF as an hour-by-hour table (see TAF decoder). The raw text is under Original.

A NOTAMs box with this aerodrome's NOTAMs from your briefing. It opens by itself when something is closed or unserviceable. Key words such as CLSD, U/S, RWY, FREQ, ACT and PJE are highlighted. Times are UTC with local time in brackets; NOTAMs starting within 24 hours are faded. If the briefing lists the aerodrome under "no current NOTAM", it says "none current". Restricted and danger areas show their status from the briefing with the reason.

Under the NOTAMs, AIP SUP / AIC lists the current AIP Supplements and Aeronautical Information Circulars for this aerodrome (its code in the title, e.g. SUP H62/26 Melbourne/Moorabbin Aerodrome (YMMB) Obstacle Infringements), and ones placed within 5 NM of it (a wind farm, a reporting point), with the dates they're in force and expire (estimated). They come from Airservices' Summary of SUP/AIC current built into the app with each AIRAC: titles and dates only. Read the SUP or AIC itself on the Airservices website (www.airservicesaustralia.com/aip/aip.asp). Items placed by a place name in their title (not an aerodrome code) are marked approximate. As the summary itself says, a SUP or AIC can start or end between summaries: check the website and NOTAMs.

Arrival (next to the ERSA button in the card's header), or Arrival card on the INBOUND CALL row, opens one screen for the aerodrome: ETA: along your flight plan, else direct at your groundspeed. Frequencies in calling order: ATIS (and whether you have the current letter), the tower (both sides for a split tower) or, when the tower is closed at your ETA, the CTAF, then ground, each with the call sign ("Moorabbin Tower", "Tyabb traffic"); the squawk when the tower is open. Runways for the wind: the wind from the ATIS you heard (Listen to ATIS), the briefing's ATIS, a recent METAR or the TAF at your ETA, in that order; each runway end with its head or tail wind and crosswind, most headwind first and ticked; and its circuit direction: right-hand where ERSA says so, otherwise left-hand (the standard). The ATIS or the traffic in the circuit decides the runway in use. ERSA notes the app picks out (circuit height, helicopter notes, CTR entry, reporting points), the aerodrome's NOTAMs and SUPs/AICs, and hover performance at your ETA when your W&B profile has hover tables.

The airspace stack above your position from the DAH steps: class G uses the area (FIA) frequency, class E the E frequency, C and D the controlling unit. Your current band is highlighted. At Avalon: SFC–A025 D Avalon Tower 120.1, A025–A045 E Avalon 133.55, A045+ C Melbourne Approach 132.0.
The Nearby list (its own tab on the full-screen map) shows aerodromes around you with distance and bearing. Tap one to show it on the card.

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: A SARTIME countdown that reminds you to cancel, spoken alerts for what's ahead, last light, and the phone settings that keep the app useful in the cockpit: keeping the screen on and lining the compass up with the aircraft.

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: More → SARTIME. Type the time in UTC (0430), or use +15 min, +1 h or Plan ETA + 30 min. A time up to an hour in the past counts as today, otherwise tomorrow. Choose who it's With: Airservices (SARTIME), or a responsible person (flight note, with their name and number under Who to call). Set SARTIME. A row in the top bar counts down: "SARTIME 0430Z in 1:20 · with ATS". Amber in the last 30 minutes, and once you've landed (stopped for 30 s after flying at 30 kt or more): "landed: cancel with ATS". Red once the time has passed ("passed 0:05 ago: cancel with ATS now"), and the phone vibrates. With spoken alerts on: "SARTIME in 15 minutes" while flying, "Landed. Remember to cancel your SARTIME.", and every 5 minutes after the time. Tap the row, then Cancelled once you've cancelled it. Clear removes it. The app cancels nothing itself. Cancel by radio or phone (numbers in ERSA), or call your responsible person.

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: Options → Spoken alerts, each on or off: Alert When Default Controlled or restricted airspace ahead When the NEXT CLASS row appears: "Class D ahead, 5 miles, Moorabbin Tower West, one two three decimal zero". Again after 10 minutes. On SIGMET / AIRMET ahead The first time one is ahead on your plan or track at your level. Again after 30 minutes. On New CTAF or area frequency When the CTAF or AREA tile changes and holds for 3 s: "Lilydale traffic, one one niner decimal one". Off SARTIME 15 minutes to go while flying, "landed", and every 5 minutes once passed. On Checklist for the phase of flight Says the checklist's name when it's offered. On Test the voice plays a sample. They use the phone's text-to-speech through the speaker or your headset. Turn the media volume up. Traffic and power line warnings are spoken separately, with Speak traffic alerts (NOTAMs (NAIPS) and traffic). "Wires ahead" is only spoken when you're under 300 ft above the ground at the line. The fuel timer has its own reminder (see Fuel timer).

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: The GS tile shows last light at your position under the speed ("last 0920Z", or "night"). Last light is the end of civil twilight (sun 6° below the horizon). From 30 minutes before, a LAST LIGHT row counts down: "LAST LIGHT in 20 min 0920Z (8:20 pm)", amber, then red from 10 minutes. After last light: "NIGHT after last light … · first light …" until first light. The pre-flight brief warns if your plan ends after last light, and the CASA fuel reserve uses day or night from it.

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: Keep screen on (More) is remembered between launches. The phone drops the lock whenever the app is hidden (screen off, switching app), so it's taken again when you come back or on your next tap. The button says Screen stays on while it holds, and Screen on: tap to re-arm if it has been lost. On older iPhones a tiny silent video keeps the screen awake instead.

pt: SARTIME, spoken alerts and the phone
t: A phone in a cradle rarely points exactly along the aircraft, and the airframe bends the compass too. The app lines the compass up with your GPS track by itself. While you fly straight and steady at 20 kt or more, it averages the difference between GPS track and compass (about 20 s to align), and adds it to the compass whenever it falls back to it (hovering, taxiing). So HDG lines up with where the nose points. The button (More) shows "Compass aligned +12°" or "aligning …%". Tap it to reset after moving the phone. It also takes in the wind correction angle at the time, so learn it into wind or in light wind. Kept until you reset it. The simulator doesn't change it. While not aligned, the button says what it's waiting for: Message Meaning under 20 kt Fly faster. not steady Track is changing; fly straight. compass unsteady Vibration, or something magnetic near the phone. compass paused Android only gives the compass to the app in front, so not in split screen. no compass No compass readings arrived. sensors blocked In Chrome allow Motion sensors for the site (the lock icon by the address, or Settings → Site settings → Motion sensors). Hold your finger on the button for the full reason. On Android the heading is worked out from the phone's full orientation, so it's right lying flat or standing upright in a cradle, in portrait or landscape.

Checklists live under Flight plan → Checklists. Tick items by tap or by voice, have the right list come up by itself at each phase of flight, and show a passenger briefing full screen. Checklist items come from your flight manual and operator's procedures. The app doesn't invent any.

The app comes with a Bell 206B3 checklist transcribed as written from an operator's sheet, in four lists: Pre start Start (with "Start – continued") Pre lift off checks Shutdown (offered after landing) You can edit or delete them. A deleted one stays deleted, also across your devices. Check them against your own operator's checklist before use.

Add your own by typing or pasting from the flight manual, one item per line. A line starting with # is a heading. Item .... response (or Item : response) puts the response on the right. Choose the aircraft (your weight and balance profiles) or every aircraft. Offer it chooses when it comes up by itself (below), or Passenger briefing. Lists combine across your devices through Google Drive and travel in the settings backup and file.
Open one and tap items to tick them. The next item is marked and the count shows at the top. Reset clears the ticks. Ticks stay on this device and survive closing the app.

Offer it Comes up when Before take-off You start moving (5 kt or more) after being stopped for a minute. Pre-landing The 10 NM inbound call fires for an aerodrome you're landing at. After landing You've stopped for 30 s after flying at 30 kt or more. The list's ticks are cleared and a CHECKLIST row shows ("Pre-landing · Before landing · tap to open") until it's complete, or for 10 minutes. Tap the row to open it. With spoken alerts on, its name is said aloud.

In a checklist, 🎙 Hands-free reads the next item aloud and listens for your response through the input picked under Radio audio and transcription. With the Whisper engine, download the speech model first. Say Does check, checked, done, next, set, on, off, complete, confirmed… or the item's own response Ticks it and reads the next. repeat, say again Reads it again. back, previous Unticks the one before. stop, cancel, pause, finish Ends hands-free. Section headings are read when they change. At the end it says "<name> complete" and stops. What the microphone hears while the tablet is speaking is ignored, so its own voice can't tick an item. A tap on an item still works. Closing the checklist stops it.

Make a checklist with Offer it: Passenger briefing and type your briefing items (from your operator's procedures or flight manual; the app has none of its own). More → Passenger brief shows them full screen, one at a time in large text with the section heading, for passengers to read with you. Tap the text or Next to go on; Back; ✕ or Esc closes. Done ticks the list and records the time. With several briefing lists for the aircraft, it shows the list to pick from. With none yet, the button starts one. A briefing list's run view also has Full screen.
Where everything in the app comes from, how sources are tagged, and what the app doesn't know. Not an authoritative source. Confirm against the current ERSA, charts, NOTAMs and ATIS.

ERSA and the DAH are the primary source for every frequency, aerodrome and airspace limit. Other data is used only where the AIP has nothing, and is tagged with its source. Every value carries a tag: green for AIP (ERSA, DAH, an AIP rule, a charted CTAF), orange for anything else. Where sources disagree, the AIP value is shown and the other mentioned as a note ("OurAirports says …"). The app never makes up or "fixes" a frequency, limit or procedure. Where the AIP is unclear (Moorabbin's two tower frequencies, for example) it shows what the AIP says and points you to the ATIS.

Source (tag) Used for ERSA (Airservices) Aerodromes, positions, elevations; CTAF, ATIS, AWIS, tower, ground, delivery, approach, departures, UNICOM; area frequency per aerodrome; tower hours; procedures and reporting points; runways (lengths, surface, width); right-hand circuits; VFR waypoints; navaid frequencies; the SUA list (restricted/danger area status, hours, activity, contacts); FAC sheets; the controlling unit for each zone and step. DAH (Airservices) All airspace (C, D, E, A, control zones, restricted, danger, military operating areas) with step limits; area (FIA) and class E frequency boundaries; broadcast areas; runway thresholds; navaids; IFR waypoints (search and simulation only). Boundaries that follow a coast, river or road are drawn as straight lines between the published points. VTC / VNC (charted CTAF) Where ERSA has no CTAF but the chart prints one beside the aerodrome, that frequency (AIP ENR 1.1 makes it the CTAF), tagged VTC, VNC or VTC/VNC with the sheet named. AIP default Any other aerodrome: CTAF 126.7, or the broadcast area frequency inside one. VATPAC The vatSys flight-sim dataset. Only names a controlling unit where ERSA has none (e.g. class A). OurAirports Strips not in ERSA (with Include non-ERSA strips on), and notes where it disagrees. XC Australia Unofficial airspace, only if no DAH is loaded. VTC / VNC chart underlay Airservices charts (39 sheets), as a picture under the app's own airspace. Fitted to their graticule within about 10 m; the app's airspace lines (from the DAH) won't sit exactly on the printed ones. WAC charts 46 old (2009) World Aeronautical Charts, under the VNC/VTC. For the picture only, not airspace or frequencies. SRTM terrain (NASA) Height above ground, AGL limits, terrain shading, profile, LSALT guide, 3D. 30″ grid (about 900 m), highest point per cell, all of Australia. EGM96 geoid Converting Android GPS height to height above mean sea level. GA coastline (Geoscience Australia, 1:100,000) Coast legs and the Coast layer. CC BY 4.0. GA power lines (Geoscience Australia) The Wires layer and warning: 66 kV and up, overhead. CC BY 4.0. Local distribution lines are not included. ABS towns and suburbs (2021) Populous areas for minimum heights, town and suburb names on the map and in search. CC BY 4.0. NAIPS briefing (Airservices) NOTAMs, METAR/TAF, ATIS, area QNH, SIGMET/AIRMET, restricted area status. Only what you loaded. RainViewer Rain radar layer (personal and educational use). adsb.lol / adsb.fi ADS-B traffic, through the proxy. Esri Satellite imagery (credit shown on the map). The VTC, VNC and ERSA are Airservices copyright.

s: AIRAC sets and the effective-date banner
t: The app carries the AIRAC data in force when it was built and, near a change, the next one. It picks whichever is in force on the phone's clock: AIRAC data takes effect at 1600 UTC the day before the effective date (AIP GEN 3.1). Both sets are stored for offline use. If the change happens while the app is open, a banner offers a reload. The effective-date banner shows when the data isn't in force yet, and the app warns when the data is more than two cycles old. The ERSA FAC sheets are from the same cycle as the frequencies on screen.

More → AIRAC changes compares the two AIP data sets the app carries (the cycle in force and the next one, or the one just ended): aerodromes added or removed and changes to their name, elevation, CTAF, ATIS, tower/ground/approach frequencies, runways, ERSA circuit directions and circuit height; airspace added, removed, or with new limits, frequency or boundary; VFR waypoints added, removed, moved or renamed; navaid frequencies and positions. Near me (within 50 NM), My plans (within 15 NM of a point on your plan or saved plans) or All. When a new pair of cycles arrives, a notice at the bottom of the screen says how many changes there are near you and on your plans, once. It compares the data as the app parses it, not the procedure text: read the ERSA and DAH amendment notes and the AIP Supplements too.

Public holidays and NOTAM changes to tower hours. Confirm on the ATIS. NOTAMs you haven't loaded. There is no live feed; get a fresh NAIPS briefing before each flight. Pressure altitude. GPS altitude is geometric, not pressure altitude. Near a step, go by the altimeter. Obstacles other than NOTAM obstacles: masts, buildings and most wires aren't in the terrain. Terrain is for awareness only. Traffic not transmitting ADS-B or not heard by a ground receiver. It isn't TCAS. Winds aloft: the NAIPS text briefing has none; enter the grid point wind yourself. Aircraft performance: W&B and hover figures are only what you enter from your flight manual. What was said on the radio: transcription mishears. It's an aid only. Local procedures beyond ERSA: check the clearance request and call wording against AIP ENR 1.1 and local procedures.

More → Flight computer is an E6B-style mechanical flight computer to practise with, in three tabs: Computer, Wind and Problems. It always shows in a dark theme. It's a training aid. Use your own computer and the app's figures for real planning.

The circular slide rule. Drag the blue disc to turn it. Drag on the outer scale to move the red cursor. Outer scale: miles or litres. Inner scale: minutes. The ▲ 60 is the speed index. An hours ring sits inside the minutes. Speed sets the index to your groundspeed (or Plan check's speed). Fuel sets it to Plan check's burn. Reset. Readout gives the values over the index and at the cursor. Untick it to practise reading the scales yourself.

Put the speed (or burn per hour) on the outer scale over the ▲ 60. Then every distance (or fuel) on the outer scale sits over its time on the inner scale. Example: 60 under 110 kt, and 55 NM sits over 30 min.

In the window at the top of the disc, set the OAT (°C, on the disc) against the pressure altitude (thousands of feet, showing through from the base). CAS on the inner scale then reads TAS on the outer scale. The DENS ALT pointer in the other window reads density altitude. Both follow the standard atmosphere (ISA), so they agree with the 120 ft per °C rule of thumb.

Red arrows on the rim. Put a value (inner scale) under one arrow and read it (inner scale) under another of the same kind: NAUT / STAT / KM, LITRES / US GAL, KG / LB. Fuel weight: put the disc's FUEL L arrow under AVGAS KG (0.72 kg/L) or JET KG (0.80 kg/L), then read kg (outer) over litres (inner). Use your fuel docket's density when you have it.

Worked the "wind dot up" way. Drag the dark ring to turn the plate. Drag inside it to slide the grid. ✎ Mark puts the wind dot: press on the centre line and slide. A label shows the knots, and the dot snaps to the centre line and to whole knots. In a problem, once the plate is on the wind a plain tap marks the dot. Erase removes it. The grid's arcs count from the grid's centre: with 100 under the grommet, 15 kt up is the 115 arc. The readout gives the course under the TRUE INDEX, the groundspeed under the grommet, and the dot's arc and drift. Crosswind shows a square grid round the grommet for crosswind and headwind components.

Choose Problems: From your flight plan (its legs, with Plan check's speed, burn and entered wind) or Random, and the Type: Type You work out Wind: heading and GS Heading, groundspeed and wind correction angle. Time from distance Time for a distance at a groundspeed. Groundspeed from time Groundspeed from a distance and time. Range Distance in a time. Fuel for a time Fuel used at a burn rate. Endurance Time from fuel and burn. Fuel burn from fuel used Burn rate from fuel used and time. Weight and balance A load sheet from your selected W&B profile with random loads (or a made-up example aircraft without one): each moment as weight × arm on the slide rule, then CG = total moment ÷ total weight, and whether it's in the envelope. The front-seat minimum and lateral limits aren't part of it. Crosswind component Crosswind and head/tailwind for a runway at a plan aerodrome or one near you, with an ATIS-style wind. Pressure altitude from QNH Elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft, at an aerodrome on your plan or near you. TAS and density altitude From pressure altitude, OAT and CAS. Conversions Distance, volume, weight and fuel weight. The steps tick themselves off as you set the computer. Hint explains the next step. Show me sets the computer to the answer (with the working for pressure altitude). Check answer compares with the app's own wind triangle and arithmetic: ±2° and ±2 kt; 2%, 1 minute or 1 L; density altitude ±400 ft; CG 0.3%. Times can be typed as minutes or h:mm. Next ▶ for another. Your score is kept.

True course 157°, TAS 90 kt, wind 270°T / 15 kt. Turn the plate until 270 is under the TRUE INDEX. Slide the grid so a convenient arc (say 100) is under the grommet, and mark the wind dot 15 kt straight up (on the 115 arc). Turn the plate until the course, 157, is under the TRUE INDEX. Slide the grid until the dot sits on the TAS arc, 90. Read the groundspeed under the grommet: about 95 kt. Read the drift at the dot: about 9° right of the centre line. The wind is from the right, so steer into it: heading = 157 + 9 = 166°T. (Wind triangle: WCA 8.8° R, GS 94.8 kt.) Apply variation for a magnetic heading.

s: Worked example: TAS and density altitude
t: Pressure altitude 4,000 ft, OAT +20 °C, CAS 100 kt. In the window, set +20 against pressure altitude 4 (thousand). Read DENS ALT: about 5,500 ft (the standard atmosphere gives 5,490). Check: ISA at 4,000 ft is +7 °C, so it's 13° above ISA; 4,000 + 13 × 120 ≈ 5,560 ft, close enough for the rule of thumb. Find 100 (CAS) on the inner scale and read TAS above it on the outer scale: about 109 kt.

Runway 17 (170°M), ATIS wind 220°M / 20 kt. Turn the plate until 220 is under the index, and mark the dot 20 kt up from the grommet. Tap Crosswind for the square grid, and turn the runway heading, 170, under the index. Read the dot: across = crosswind, up = headwind (down = tailwind). Here the wind is 50° off the runway: about 15 kt crosswind from the right and 13 kt headwind. (20 × sin 50° = 15.3; 20 × cos 50° = 12.9.)
Load a GPX route or build one on the phone. The active waypoint moves on by itself like a GNSS navigator, and the aerodrome card, frequencies and alerts follow the plan.

Import GPX: pick a route exported from OzRunways, AvPlan or similar. It reads the route points; without a route, the waypoints; then a track (thinned to 60 points). Each point is matched to the AIP by name and position, e.g. "RLR VFR waypoint · Rosslynne Resv". Unmatched points keep their GPX description. Save GPX: downloads the plan as it is now, edits included, as a GPX route named like YBRS-YMMB-2026-10-28.gpx, with your leg altitudes and land marks. It opens in OzRunways or AvPlan, or here again. The plan is kept on the phone until you remove it or load another.

The panel shows the active waypoint with bearing °M, distance, cross-track error (L/R), ETE at your groundspeed, leg course, and distance and time to go. The leg list gives each leg's course, distance and suggested altitude. Tap a leg to make it active. Buttons: Prev, Next, Edit, Reverse, Remove, Save GPX, Share, Flight log, Plan check and Weight & balance. In the header: New plan, Plans, Waypoints, Checklists, Import GPX. On the map the route is purple with each leg's track and distance in a box.

Tap Edit (or New plan with none loaded). Add: the search box uses the same fuzzy search as Go to. Tap a match or press Enter; the box stays open. The menu beside it says where it goes: at end, best fit (least added distance) or as next (it becomes the active waypoint). From the map: press and hold → Start flight plan at …, Insert … after … or Add … at end of plan. Reorder and delete: ▲ and ▼ move a point, ✕ deletes it. The active waypoint stays the same point. Replace: ⇄ marks a point; the next point you pick (search, or Replace … with … in the map menu) takes its place. Tap ⇄ again to cancel. Land / no land: each aerodrome has a Land toggle (the last point is Land by default; a LAND tag shows in the list). This decides inbound vs transit calls, squawk, and where Plan check and hover performance look. Altitude override: each leg has an altitude box. Type 2500, A045, FL095, or 45 (= 4,500 ft). Empty goes back to the suggestion. The app warns when your altitude is below the minimum height, above the controlled airspace base less your buffer, or not a VFR table level at 3,000 ft and above ("2,500 !"). Tap Done to finish. The original GPX file isn't changed. Reverse turns the plan round for the trip home.

In Edit, the ≈ button on a waypoint makes the leg to it follow the coast a set distance off the shore. ≈ Coast legs settings: offset 300, 500, 1,000 or 1,500 ft, 0.5 or 1 NM (default 500 ft); gap none, 0.5, 1, 2, 3 or 5 NM (default 2 NM). The gap is the most open water it hops straight across (the Rip, river mouths, bay entrances) instead of following it in. The route is worked out on the phone from Geoscience Australia's 1:100,000 coastline and goes into the plan as turn points CST1, CST2… (hidden in the list and map except the next one). The next-waypoint panel, profile, Plan check and GPX follow it. From or to an inland point (Moorabbin, Carrum) the route meets the coast close by and follows it. Tap ≈ again for a direct leg. Changing a setting redoes every coast leg. Editing works a coast leg out again when the change touches it (a new start, a point added among its turn points, its end replaced, the point before it moved or deleted). Adding at the end or reversing leaves it as is. Offline: the whole coastline (about 1.6 MB) downloads in the background the first time you have signal. ≈ Coast legs shows how much is stored, with Store now while some is missing. Turn points are saved with the plan, so flying a coast leg never needs the coastline; only making or changing one does. Plan check, TOT and the inbound call treat a coast leg as one leg to its end. Coast legs are for planning, not terrain or obstacle clearance. Check the chart.

Plans keeps plans on the phone by name. Save current plan (with altitudes and land marks). Saving under an existing name replaces it (it asks first). Load one later, or ⇄ to load it backwards. Loading asks first if your current plan isn't saved. With six or more plans a find box appears (name, or a point such as YTYA). Saved plans travel in the settings backup and settings file, and combine across phones through Google Drive.

Share (in the plan buttons, or beside a saved plan) shows a link and QR code with the plan inside it: points, leg altitudes, land / overfly, and coast legs with their settings. Opening the link or scanning the code on another phone asks, then loads it. Nothing is uploaded. Copy link, Share… and Save GPX are in the same box.

The active waypoint moves on, like a GNSS navigator, when: you're within 0.5 NM of it; you cross the turn bisector at it within 5 NM (passing a mile or two off track, or cutting the corner, still counts); you leave the first point of the plan; catch-up: after a GPS gap, you're clearly on a later leg (within 2 NM of it and tracking along it). A waypoint picked by hand (Prev, Next, a leg tap) only sequences within 0.5 NM until you've flown 1 NM towards it. Every change is written to the flight log.

With a plan loaded, choosing a Go to yourself (search, or Go to in the map menu) is a direct-to: Go to, PLAN (labelled DIRECT), the next-frequency lines and the simulator all point at it, and the plan is paused. The flight plan shows "Direct to … Plan paused at 4/13 YMMB" with Resume plan; the Go to bar has Resume plan in place of Clear. Choosing a point that is in the plan (e.g. YLIL) just makes it the next waypoint, with no pause. A direct-to aerodrome counts as a landing (inbound call, tower, squawk) until you resume. Prev, Next or a leg tap also ends it. It's remembered across restarts.

Under the next-waypoint panel, the whole route side-on: terrain (highest point in each 30″ cell), controlled airspace and restricted/danger areas from the DAH with each base as a solid line, waypoints as dashed lines, and you when within 5 NM of the route; a red line where terrain comes within 1,000 ft of the airspace base above it; suggested leg altitudes in purple, the minimum height as a red dashed line, populous areas as a grey strip; + and − set the top altitude (1,000 to 25,000 ft); Auto fits the route; tap for the distance, leg, terrain and airspace stack at that point. The summary gives the highest terrain, lowest controlled-airspace base, control zones from the surface you cross, and the tightest terrain-to-base gap. Terrain is along straight legs and the grid can miss a narrow peak or mast. It's for planning awareness, not obstacle clearance.

VFR levels from AIP ENR 1.7 Table B by magnetic track: 000–179° 1,500, 3,500, 5,500…; 180–359° 2,500, 4,500, 6,500…. The table applies at 3,000 ft and above; below that a non-table altitude is offered when no table level fits (orange). Minimum height (CASR 91.265/91.267, MOS 12.01 note): over populous areas 1,000 ft above the highest terrain within 600 m (300 m for helicopters); elsewhere 500 ft above the highest terrain within 300 m. Not counted within 2 NM of the first and last aerodrome. Ceiling: the base of class C, D or A less a buffer (500 ft by default). Class E isn't a ceiling; the note says when you'd be in E. The control zone of the aerodrome at either end of a leg is left out. Flagged red: "split" (needs different levels along the leg: add a waypoint), or "!" (minimum height above the airspace limit: get a clearance or re-route). Masts and buildings are not in the data. Check the VTC/VNC.

Press and hold the map → Save as waypoint…, give it a name (e.g. FUEL DRUM) and an optional note. It shows as a ★ on the map (tap for its menu), comes up in search and Go to, and can go in plans. Waypoints lists them (go to, edit, delete), with Add where I am and Add by position (-38.1234, 144.5678 or S38 12.3 E144 30.1). They're in the settings backup and file, and combine across phones through Google Drive.

Type in Go to (or the simulator's Position) for a pick list as you type. It searches aerodromes, VFR waypoints, navaids, IFR waypoints, your ★ waypoints, towns and suburbs. Fuzzy: prefixes, any word, substrings, small typos ("geelng"), no spaces ("stkilda"), letters in order. Aerodromes and nearby places rank first. Phonetic alphabet: "yankee lima india lima" finds YLIL, "charlie alpha romeo romeo" CARR. A leading "go to" or "direct to" is ignored. Mic button: say a place or spell a code. What you said goes in the box with the list open; tap the match to confirm. Chrome on the phone recognises speech on the device where it can (it downloads its English pack once with signal). Offline without that, use the keyboard's mic (Gboard voice typing works offline). The Go to bar shows bearing (°M), distance and an arrow; the map draws a dotted line and a target. It's kept until you clear it. A plain map tap never sets Go to.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: A fuel timer and range circle for the flight, and a weight and balance calculator with your own aircraft's figures. The app never invents aircraft data: the numbers come from your flight manual and weighing report.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: More → Fuel timer (or tap the FUEL row). Enter Fuel on board and Burn (L or L/h; US gal with a lb W&B profile), and optionally Reserve min (empty = CASA's final reserve at your position and time). Set fuel now starts the count from that amount. Start / Stop runs and pauses it. Start and stop by itself: starts when you're moving at 40 kt or more, stops after 3 minutes below 5 kt. Fuel check reminder: off, or every 15, 20 or 30 min, spoken with a vibration while the timer runs. The FUEL row in the top bar shows fuel left, and time and distance to your reserve at your groundspeed. Amber under 30 minutes to reserve, red at it. Fuel left = what you set minus burn × time the timer has run. It's an estimate. Dip or gauge the tanks.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: The Range map layer draws a circle round you at the distance you can fly before reaching your reserve at your groundspeed now, and a dashed circle at half that labelled OUT & BACK. It opens the fuel timer if that isn't set. With a wind known (the GPS estimate while flying, or the wind in Plan check) the ring leans downwind, showing the least and most you can go.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: Weight & balance sits next to Plan check in the flight plan. Set up your aircraft once, then type each load.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: Under Aircraft profile (from the POH and weighing report): units kg·mm·L or lb·in·USG; empty weight, arm and lateral arm from the weighing report; maximum take-off weight; stations (seats, baggage, fuel tanks, fixed items) with their arms, limits and tank capacities, and fuel density; the CG envelope corners from the flight manual, one "arm, weight" per line, and optional lateral limits; Hover ceiling IGE and Hover ceiling OGE (see below). Keep several aircraft: Aircraft picks one; New profile, Copy and Delete (asks for a second tap). New from starts from a template: Bell 206B-3 (91 gal) and Bell 206A/B (76 gal): stations, fuel and limits from Bell's publications (lb/in, Jet A). The empty weight and arm are left empty for your own aircraft's weighing record. Bell 206B (weighed): kg/mm/L, with one individual aircraft's weighing figures. Replace them with your own aircraft's weighing report. Blank. The numbers are yours to check against your flight manual and your aircraft's current weighing report.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: A table of stations with a weight box, arm, moment and can add (the most you could still put there with everything else as loaded). Weights in lb or kg and Fuel in US gal, litres or (where the profile has a gauge table) gauge reading. Results stay in the profile's units. Empty weight and fixed items (e.g. engine oil) are always counted.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: Take-off, landing (after the plan's fuel, at Plan check's GS and burn) and zero-fuel weight and CG against the envelope, and the whole burn line in between. A plot of the envelope with the loading path station by station (and the lateral chart where the profile has lateral limits). The most fuel you can carry (and the endurance), and the fuel for the plan plus the final reserve. Fixes when out of limits: less fuel, move or leave out bags, swap passengers (never the pilot), add weight on the other side, or how much to offload. A front-seat minimum, where the profile has one, gets its own line. Plan check shows the result too.

pt: Fuel, weight and balance, hover performance
t: Each W&B profile has two boxes: Hover ceiling IGE (in ground effect) Hover ceiling OGE (out of ground effect) Type one line per point, density altitude ft, max weight, copied from your flight manual's hover ceiling charts, in the profile's weight units. Read several points off the chart (for instance at every 1,000 or 2,000 ft of density altitude across the range you fly) : a density altitude outside your table shows red. Use the chart for the configuration you fly (engine, doors, etc.). Nothing is built in. Without these lines the table shows density altitude only. The app interpolates in a straight line between your points and never extrapolates past the first or last one. With them, the pre-flight brief has a Hover performance table for the departure and every point you land at: temperature, QNH, pressure and density altitude, your weight there, the IGE and OGE limits and the margin. Amber under 5% margin; red over the limit or outside your table. See Pre-flight brief. Density altitude in the app is an approximation (pressure altitude + 120 ft per °C above ISA). The flight manual's charts govern.

Install the app, let it store its data for offline use, and learn the three screen layouts. The app is built for and tested on a Google Pixel 9 Pro (Chrome on Android); iPhones and 8–10" Android tablets work too.

Open the app's address in Chrome. Tap Install app (in the More buttons, or Chrome's ⋮ menu → Install app). Open the installed app and tap Start GPS & compass. Allow location and keep Precise on. The installed app runs full screen and Android keeps its stored data.

Open the same address in Safari and tap Start. Share → Add to Home Screen. On iPhone use the Home Screen app, not a Safari tab. Safari can clear a website's stored data after a few weeks without visits, which would remove your offline data and settings.

s: First launch and the loading screen
t: While the app starts, a loading screen lists each step (aerodromes and airspace with the ERSA date, towns and suburbs, app code) with the amount received, and says whether it is loading from offline storage. If something can't load, it shows which step failed and why. It also shows what is stored for use without signal: Terrain tiles (all of Australia, about 11 MB) Coastline areas (about 1.6 MB, used by coast legs and the Coast layer) Chart sheets you have picked (the Melbourne VNC and VTC by default) Power lines Each row has a count, and a line under them gives the download speed, what is left and roughly how long, e.g. "about 1.2 MB/s · 9.6 MB to go · about 8 s". The time is an estimate from the number of items stored and their average size. The first time (or after new content) it stays until everything is stored. Start now opens the app straight away and the downloads carry on in the background. The footer's Offline line shows how they're going. With everything already stored, it closes as soon as the app is ready. Without signal, it starts after a few seconds with what is there.

After one load with signal everything below works without a connection: GPS, compass, the map, charts you've ticked, terrain, coastline, search, the elevation profile, flight plans, checklists, the flight log and (once its model is downloaded) transcription. Needs signal: live ADS-B traffic, satellite imagery you haven't viewed before, rain radar, Google Drive saves, and opening NAIPS. NOTAMs and weather come from the NAIPS briefing you load, which is then kept on the phone. Check you're ready: the footer at the bottom of the page shows what is stored ("ready to fly without signal" when it's all there). The pre-flight brief also has a Ready to fly without signal? check for your route (see Pre-flight brief). Weak signal: the app waits up to 3 seconds for the network, then starts from the stored copy, so a poor connection in flight doesn't hold it up. ERSA FAC sheets are stored when first opened. The sheets for your plan and Go to aerodromes are fetched in the background while you have signal.

Updates arrive the next time you open the app with signal. If an update lands while the app is open, a bar says App updated · tap to reload. Tap it to switch to the new version. Which version you have: the footer starts with "App updated <date and time> (<how long ago>)". If it's older than you expect, close the app and open it again with signal. The app carries the current AIRAC data and, near a cycle change, the next one. It switches by itself at 1600 UTC the day before the effective date (see AIRAC sets).

Try the app on the ground without GPS. Tap Simulate (in More) to open the simulator panel: Position accepts decimal degrees (-38.04, 144.47; a missing minus is taken as south), DMS (38 02 22S 144 28 10E), degrees and minutes (3802.4S 14428.2E), an aerodrome code (YMAV), a VFR waypoint (CARR or CARRUM), a navaid ident (AV) or an IFR waypoint. Alt (ft), Track (°M) and GS (kt) apply as you type. No Enter needed. Fly moves you along the track at the groundspeed. With a flight plan loaded it flies the route; typing a track takes over until you press Fly again. From the map's press-and-hold menu, Move simulator here jumps the simulator to that point. Replay GPX plays a recorded flight back through the app (see Replay). You can also start the simulator from the address: add ?sim=YMMB&alt=1000&trk=110&gs=0 to the app's address. sim= takes the same kinds of position as the Position box. Nothing is logged in the simulator, and it doesn't change your compass alignment. The GPS tile is orange with SIM under it. Simulated altitudes are taken as above mean sea level.

Once GPS (or the simulator) is running the map fills the screen. The key tiles float over the map: CTAF and AREA top left (with the dashed → tiles when you have a Go to or plan), and the alert rows under them. GPS, ALT, TRK, GS and CLASS are top right. Heading tape A runs across the top. Tap a floating tile for the whole top bar; ▲ Back to the map closes it. The sheet at the bottom holds everything else in tabs: Aerodrome, Radio calls, Flight plan, Go to, Legend, NOTAMs, Nearby and More. Tap a tab to open the sheet half way at that section; tap it again to close. Drag the tab bar to settle it closed, half or nearly full. Zoom, Traffic, Layers, Track up and ⤡ float on the map's right edge.

⤡ goes back to the classic page: the top bar, then the map, then Go to, simulator, flight plan, aerodrome card, Nearby and settings, all on one scrolling page. ⤢ returns to full screen. Options → Map → Full-screen map sets which one you start in.

The whole top bar is a column on the left and the map fills the rest at full height. The splitter: drag the grip on the edge between the column and the map to make the column wider or narrower (240 px up to 45% of the screen). Arrow keys work too. The width is kept. Alert rows sit at the top of the column so they never scroll out of sight. A tablet held upright uses the phone's full-screen layout. On the classic page, tablets in portrait get a two-column layout, and in landscape the map is fixed on the left with everything else scrolling on the right. Tiles can be turned on or off separately for the phone layout and the tablet-landscape layout: Options → Top bar tiles (see Top bar).

Radio Calls AU is a phone and tablet app for VFR pilots in Australia, built with helicopters in mind. It tells you who to talk to, on what frequency, and what to say, wherever you are, and it works without signal once it has loaded.

Where you are: the closest aerodrome (or the next one on your plan) with its CTAF, ATIS/AWIS, tower and approach frequencies, the area frequency, and the airspace class, cap and lower limit at your altitude. What's ahead: alerts when controlled or restricted airspace starts within 10 NM ahead, a SIGMET is on your track, terrain or power lines are close, or traffic is near. What to say: a radio call guide that switches between CTAF and Class D procedures, inbound and transit call reminders, and your own wording. A moving map: airspace, CTAF areas, VTC/VNC/WAC charts, terrain, satellite imagery, NOTAMs, ADS-B traffic, your flight plan and log. Planning: GPX flight plans or plans built on the phone, coast legs, a pre-flight brief, fuel, weight and balance, hover performance. In the cockpit: SARTIME countdown, checklists, a read-back pad, spoken alerts, offline radio transcription, a flight computer to practise with, and a flight log and logbook.

Not an authoritative source. Confirm everything against the current ERSA, charts, NOTAMs and ATIS before you rely on it. The AIP (ERSA and DAH) comes first. Every frequency, aerodrome and airspace limit is taken from ERSA and the DAH. Anything from another source is used only where the AIP has nothing, and is tagged with where it came from (VATPAC, OurAirports, XC Australia). See Data sources. The app never makes up or "fixes" a frequency, limit or procedure. Where the AIP is unclear it shows what the AIP says and points you to the ATIS, ERSA or NOTAMs. Check the effective date. A banner shows when the data isn't in force yet, and the app warns when it is more than two cycles old. GPS altitude is geometric, not pressure altitude. Near an airspace step, go by your altimeter and the chart. Terrain is for awareness only. It is a 30 arc-second grid without buildings, masts or most wires. It is not terrain or obstacle clearance. Transcription and suggestions are an aid only. The speech model mishears callsigns and numbers. Your ears and your read-back come first, and nothing is filled in until you tap it. Traffic is not TCAS. Internet ADS-B is late and patchy at low level. Keep looking out. NOTAMs come only from the NAIPS briefing you load. Get a fresh one before each flight. Tower hours are read from ERSA. Public holidays and NOTAM changes aren't known to the app: confirm on the ATIS.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: The app records every flight on the device, works out your flight times for the logbook, and can save it all to your own Google Drive.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Every GPS fix (one per 5 s) and each waypoint change is stored on the device as it happens, and kept for 90 days. With Traffic on, ADS-B traffic is saved too; with transcription on, each transcribed transmission with time and position. The simulator is never logged. Flight log (under the plan's leg list) downloads the last 6 hours as GPX. The map's Log layer shows the same 6 hours.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: More → Logbook (or Options → Logbook and flight logs (kept 90 days)) lists each flight (fixes split at gaps over 30 minutes) with date, time and length. GPX downloads that flight, with its traffic tracks and radio transcripts (as waypoints named "Radio 0412Z"). CSV downloads a logbook file for that flight. ▶ replays it (see Replay).

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Each flight is split into legs from the GPS: Off when groundspeed reaches 20 kt. On at the start of a stop under 5 kt lasting 3 minutes or more, or the end of the log. From / to: the aerodrome within 3 NM, a helicopter landing site within 1 NM, else the coordinates. Each leg shows off and on times, airborne time (h:mm), distance and maximum altitude. Night is the time after last light and before first light (civil twilight) at the departure point. A hover taxi or a hover of 3 minutes or more reads as a landing. Check the times before copying them into your logbook.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Each leg has Edit: change From / To and the number of landings; Merge with next leg (a hover taxi or long hover that split one flight in two); Split again undoes it; Not a flight: struck out, left out of totals and CSV.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Totals for the last 7, 28 and 365 days: hours, legs, landings, night. A short summary of each leg is kept for good (beyond the 90 days of fixes), so the 365-day total keeps counting. Logbook CSV ("CSV: all N legs since …") has every leg ever logged on this device: date, aircraft (your callsign), type, from, to, UTC and local times, h:mm, decimal hours, day and night hours, landings, NM and max altitude.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: ▶ next to a flight, or Replay GPX in the simulator (a Flight log download or any GPX with timed points). Play at 1×, 2×, 5× or 10×, pause, or drag the slider. The app runs exactly as in flight (tiles, alerts, reminders, map) in simulator mode, so nothing is logged. Radio transcripts show on the RADIO row at their time. The app's clock isn't shifted: tower hours, last light and NOTAMs are for now, not the time of the flight.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Options → Google Drive → Connect Google Drive signs in once. With Save after each flight on (the default), a few minutes after a flight ends (35 minutes with no movement), when there's signal, the app saves to a Radio Calls AU folder in your Drive: one GPX per flight (with traffic and radio transcripts), e.g. Flight 2026-11-06 0912.gpx; Logbook.csv, rewritten with every leg ever logged (it reads the Drive copy first and keeps legs it doesn't have); Settings backup.json: aircraft, W&B, saved plans, waypoints, checklists, call wording and options. Not your NAIPS login, Drive sign-in or satellite key. Flights from before you connected count too. The device keeps 90 days of flights; on connecting (or reconnecting) every one not already in the folder is saved. Connect within 90 days of a flight to keep it. Save now saves straight away. Restore settings loads the backup. Disconnect removes the sign-in and withdraws access; the files stay in Drive. The app can only see the files it made. Your sign-in is kept on the device, encrypted. Drive needs a one-off setup of your own Google sign-in client and the proxy. See the project README if Connect doesn't work.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Every device signed in to the same Google account uses the same folder. Connecting another device: if Drive already has a settings backup, the app asks first whether to use it here (it reloads with those settings). Say no and the Drive backup is left alone until you tap Save now on that device. Saved plans, your waypoints and checklists combine across devices: one saved on either appears on both, and one deleted on one is removed from the others. Other settings are whichever device saved last. Each device's logbook legs stay in Logbook.csv.

pt: Flight log, logbook and Google Drive
t: Options → Settings file: Export settings saves aircraft, W&B, plans, call wording and options to a .json file. No passwords or keys; no logs or charts. Import settings reads that file on any device after you confirm, then reloads the app.
The airspace map shows where you are against airspace, CTAF areas, charts, terrain and your plan. This page covers moving it around, the press-and-hold menu, and every layer.

Pan: drag with one finger. While panned the map stays put as you move. Tap ◎ Centre to go back to your position. Zoom: pinch with two fingers (2.5 to 320 NM), or use − and + to step through 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 NM. On a computer, the mouse wheel. Rotate: turn two fingers. It only starts turning after a definite twist, so a pinch alone doesn't rotate it. The button then shows which way is up, e.g. 092° up. North up / Track up: the button switches between them. A map turned by hand goes to north up. While panned, track up holds the track of that moment rather than following you. Press and hold (right-click on a computer) opens the map menu for that point. See below. The map uses a projection that keeps everything at its true bearing from the centre; distances on screen are within about 0.1% out to 380 NM. Zoomed out to 160 or 320 NM, aerodrome dots get smaller, and the CTAF layer, NOTAM circles, waypoints and labels only show at 80 NM and closer.

A plain tap never changes your Go to. This stops an accidental tap overriding a flight plan. Tap an aerodrome: it becomes the aerodrome on the Aerodrome card (frequencies, calls). The CTAF tile shows a CARD YMMB ✕ badge; tap the ✕ (or Back to auto on the card) to go back to the closest aerodrome. Tap a VFR waypoint, navaid or one of your own ★ waypoints: its menu opens. Choose Go to there if you want it. Tap a traffic target: selects it (see Traffic). While measuring: a tap adds a measure point.

Hold a finger still on the map for about half a second (right-click on a computer). A crosshair marks the point and the menu shows: Where it is: the nearest town, locality or suburb ("1.6 NM N of Seville East"). Its position: degrees and decimal minutes plus decimal lat/lon, distance and bearing from you, terrain height there. Frequencies there, in two groups: the nearest aerodrome within 10 NM: CTAF, ATIS or AWIS, TWR (split towers with the side the point is on underlined), GND, DEL, APP, DEP, UNICOM and the ERSA area frequency. Tower-only frequencies are struck through outside tower hours. With no aerodrome nearby, the broadcast area CTAF or 126.7; Airspace here, SFC up: every band over the point with its frequency, unit and limits. The band at your altitude is outlined. Special use airspace there: every prohibited, restricted, danger and military operating area at all levels, with DAH limits, ERSA hours (HJ, H24, NOTAM explained), activity, the controlling authority with a tap-to-call number, and the RA1/RA2/RA3 status with what ERSA says it means. With a briefing loaded, its NOTAM status too. NOTAMs whose circle covers the point, obstacles within 1 NM, and any SIGMET/AIRMET there. Buttons: Go to this point, or Go to the nearest aerodrome, VFR waypoint or navaid within 2 NM. With a plan loaded this is a direct-to (see Direct to). Start flight plan at … (no plan), or Insert … after … (where it adds the least distance) and Add … at end of plan. Within 0.3 NM of an aerodrome, waypoint or navaid, that point is added instead of a bare position. In Edit, Replace … with …. Measure from … / Measure to …. Save as waypoint… (or Edit / Delete on one of your ★ waypoints). Copy lat/lon, and in the simulator Move simulator here. Close it by tapping elsewhere, dragging the map, or ✕. On the full-screen map the menu always sits above the tiles, and the sheet closes so it has room.

On the full-screen map, the Layers button (stacked sheets, beside Traffic and North up) opens a grid of layer buttons over the map. It stays open while you switch layers; tap anywhere else to close it. On the classic page the buttons are in a row under the map. Each choice is remembered. Button What it shows Default CTAF Each aerodrome's 10 NM CTAF area and the DAH broadcast areas, coloured by frequency. Details below. Off Terrain Terrain shading and warnings. Details below. On Sat Esri satellite imagery under the airspace. Needs a proxy or an Esri key (Options → Satellite imagery). Off Charts The VTC/VNC/WAC chart underlay. Details below. On Lead An orange dashed line 10 NM ahead along your track (or compass heading when slow), a cross line every NM and every second one numbered. On Wires The 66 kV and up transmission network (Geoscience Australia), with pylon ticks, dashed where under construction, voltage at 10 NM. Shows at 40 NM and closer. Off Coast The coastline and islands as a teal line, from the stored coastline data. Shows up to 160 NM range. Off Radar The latest RainViewer rain radar image, with its time and age bottom left (red over 30 min old). Online only. Off Measure Measure distances and bearings. Details below. Off Range Fuel range circle from the fuel timer (see Range circle). Off Log Your track over the last 6 hours, coloured by altitude. Off Wx Flight category rings round aerodromes from your briefing (see Weather rings). On Side A side view strip of terrain and airspace for the next 20 NM. Off Traffic ADS-B traffic (separate button; see Traffic). Off

Each aerodrome gets a 10 NM area (the AIP CTAF call distance). Areas on the same frequency merge into one shape with one colour. The AIP default 126.7 is grey so specific CTAFs stand out. A tower aerodrome gets its whole control zone instead of a circle, on its after-hours CTAF (Moorabbin 118.1, Avalon 120.1), or on the tower frequency labelled TWR where there is no CTAF. Up to eight frequencies in view get different colours. There's no red, orange or magenta: those are for restricted and danger areas. Split overlapping CTAF areas (Options, on): where two aerodromes with different CTAFs are under 20 NM apart, their circles are cut halfway between them. The CTAF tile changes at the same line. Split 126.7 areas too (off) includes the grey 126.7 circles in the split.

Terrain at or above your altitude is red; within 500 ft below you, amber (cross-hatched red and hatched orange in rainbow mode). Rainbow topographic terrain (Options, on by default): ground coloured by height from teal at sea level through green, yellow, orange and red to purple on the highest ranges (about 7,000 ft). Untick it for grey relief. Over a chart or satellite imagery only the warnings are drawn. Terrain is for awareness only. Each 30″ cell (about 900 m) holds the highest SRTM point in it; buildings, masts and wires aren't included.

s: Chart underlay and the chart picker
t: Charts turns the underlay on and off. Chart underlay (in the Legend tab, or under the map on the classic page) opens a pop-up with the opacity slider, import, Turn on every chart in this view and Choose charts…. All 39 Airservices VTC/VNC sheets are available (except the Tindal VNC and the Sydney inset VTC), plus 46 old (2009) WACs drawn under them. The Melbourne VNC and VTC download by default. Choose charts in Options → Chart downloads (VNC / VTC / WAC): a map of Australia shows every chart's area: ticked ones filled, others dashed, your current map view in red. Tap an area to tick or untick the smallest chart there; Tick charts in this map view, Only charts in this view (asks first; unticked charts' tiles are removed), Tick charts along the flight plan; tabs All / VTC / VNC / WAC / Ticked, and a search box that finds a chart by name or by a place on it (YMMB, Mildura); tap a chart's small map (⌖) to show it on the main map for 10 seconds, without ticking it. You can import a newer Airservices PDF on the phone; it replaces the built-in sheet until removed. WACs are old editions: use them for the picture, not for airspace or frequencies.

Tap Measure, then tap points (aerodromes and waypoints snap to their exact position). It shows each leg's distance and magnetic bearing, the total, the time at your groundspeed, and you to the last point. From me starts at your position; Undo, Clear, Done. Dragging still pans.

Your track over the last 6 hours, coloured by altitude (blue near the surface through green and yellow to red at 6,000 ft and above), fading with age and broken at gaps. A ring marked →4 shows where the plan moved on to waypoint 4. In the simulator the simulated track shows in grey and isn't stored.

A strip at the bottom of the map with the next 20 NM along your plan (or your track, or heading when stopped): terrain, airspace steps and restricted/danger areas in map colours, and your altitude as a dashed orange line. Terrain within 500 ft of your altitude or above it is red, and a dashed line marks where your altitude would enter class A, C, D or a restricted area. Power lines you'll cross are a small mast mark at the ground (amber when you're under 500 ft above the ground there); NOTAM obstacles within 0.5 NM are drawn up to their height (red when within 300 ft of your altitude). The caption says what and how far ("class D in 5.5 NM · power line in 4.1 NM (534 ft above the ground there)"). ✕ closes it. The flight plan's elevation profile shows the same marks for the whole plan.

Chart conventions: C solid blue, D and CTR dashed blue, E violet, restricted areas red, danger areas dashed orange. Area frequency boundaries are dotted green with the frequency inside. Labels give class, then upper over lower limit, and sit wholly inside their area. The airspace you're in at your altitude is shaded. Only airspace starting below FL125, or below 5,000 ft above you, is drawn. Highlight the area you're in (Options, on): the control zone you're inside gets a bold edge; otherwise the CTAF area of the aerodrome on the CTAF tile gets a bold green ring, with a dot at its nearest edge and edge 2.9 NM. Runways are drawn at 5 NM and closer, labelled at 2.5 NM. Towns show at 20 NM and below, localities at 10 NM, suburbs at 5 NM; they're hidden while a chart shows.

In the sheet's Legend tab (under the map on the classic page). Tap an item (C, D / CTR, E, R, Danger, Area freq boundary, VFR waypoint, Terrain, Navaids) to hide or show it; hidden items are struck through and remembered. Navaids (NDB, VOR, DME, VOR/DME, TACAN) are hidden by default. Tap Navaids to show them (at 20 NM and closer). They can still be found with search either way. The CTAF legend lists the frequencies in view; the Log, Wx and rainbow terrain legends show while those layers are on.

Selected aerodrome line: dashed orange from your aircraft to the card's aerodrome, with a box such as 227°/5NM ▶ (magnetic bearing / whole NM). Flight plan: purple route with waypoint labels; the active waypoint filled in. Leg boxes: each leg has a box with its magnetic track and distance ("204°/15NM", one decimal under 10 NM). A coast leg gets one box, e.g. "coast/57NM". The active leg's box has a thicker edge. Go to target: a purple target with the name at the end of the dotted Go to line. Off the map, a small target with an arrow at the edge, e.g. CATANI 29 NM. Your aircraft: arrow, 2-blade helicopter or fixed wing, in five sizes (Options → Map → Your aircraft). Your own waypoints: ★ with their names.

Options → Map → Heading display. Each style shows your track in °M (the compass heading, marked HDG, when you're slow), a filled magenta bug for the wind-corrected heading to steer to the next waypoint or Go to, and a hollow bug for the straight bearing. A · Tape at the top (default): a tape across the top of the screen, with "STEER 030 · turn left 10° → CARR 8.4 NM" under it where there's room. C · Arc round your aircraft: a 110° compass arc on the map round your symbol. D · Tape in the nav tiles: a compact tape in place of the HDG and →HDG tiles. Or A + C, C + D, or Off. See also the nav row.

All from the NAIPS briefing you load (see Weather and NOTAMs). NOTAM circles: airspace and warning NOTAMs (restricted area activations, parachuting, drones) as dashed red circles, labelled at 40 NM and closer. Temporary zones: NOTAM areas with three or more coordinates as red dashed polygons, dimmer in the 3 hours before they start. Restricted/danger areas: active ones get a stronger fill and an "ACT →1300Z" line; those that are off are thin grey dashed, labelled OFF. Obstacles: tower symbols at their NOTAM position within 20 NM range, height (ft AMSL) at 10 NM and closer, red when within 300 ft of your altitude or above it. SIGMET/AIRMET: amber long dashes with the phenomenon and levels, the label placed inside the area.

Options → Map → 3D view (development) opens a floating window with a 3D view around you (up to 40 NM). Drag the title bar to move it and the corner to resize. Camera: Cockpit (drag to look around), Chase, or Orbit (drag, pinch or scroll). Double-tap or ⟲ resets. Surface: Chart, Relief or Satellite. Layers: Airspace walls, Clearance (terrain at or above you red, within 500 ft amber), Plan, Traffic, Obstacles. Preview ▶: flies your plan at its leg altitudes, ending at circuit height over the destination (500 ft above it for a helicopter, 1,000 ft for an aeroplane). 10, 20 or 40 NM per minute. The 3D view is a work in progress, for trying out only. Not for navigation.

A tour of every setting. On the full-screen map, the More tab holds the buttons below, including Options. On the classic page they're in the buttons row. All settings are kept on the device and travel in the settings backup and file (except passwords and keys).

Which chart sheets download and stay on the device: the map of Australia, Tick charts in this map view, Only charts in this view, Tick charts along the flight plan, tabs and search. Default: Melbourne VNC and VTC. New sheets appear unticked, marked NEW. See Chart underlay.
Flights with GPX, CSV and ▶ replay; leg edits; totals; Logbook CSV. See Logbook.
Connect Google Drive, Save now, Restore settings, Disconnect, and Save after each flight (default on). See Google Drive.
Traffic distance: 10–100 NM (default 25). Traffic symbol size: Small to Largest (default Normal).

Controlled or restricted airspace ahead (on), SIGMET / AIRMET ahead (on), New CTAF or area frequency (off), SARTIME (on), Checklist for the phase of flight (on), and Test the voice. See Spoken alerts.

Audio input test: List inputs, Listen, Raw audio (on), Record 30 s, Play back, Save recording. Transcribe the input (off), Alert when my callsign is heard (on), Check my read-back (on), Sensitivity (Low / Normal / High). Transcribe the recording, Copy, Clear, and the log. See Radio audio and transcription.
Export settings / Import settings. See Settings file.

Flash CTAF and AREA when they change: number of pulses (default 5; 0 = off). Every tile and alert row, with an example and two ticks (phone / tablet landscape). All on by default. Tap a tile to enlarge it (on). See Top bar.
